prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val][adversarial] Feature matrix with long row headers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Capability" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 411px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 36px
  col 3: header "Team" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 4: header "Business" · longest unbreakable word 72px · one-line width 72px
  col 5: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 83px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 510px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 509px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 510px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"A plan-comparison feature matrix: readers check whether a capability exists in each of four plans (Free → Enterprise), so the primary task is scanning a row rightward and comparing the tick/dash pattern across plans, with the capability name as the anchor.","reading":"Readers enter on the left row header, read the capability phrase as a unit, then sweep across the four mark columns to find the first plan that includes it. Vertical comparison of the mark columns is secondary but matters for 'what does Enterprise add' questions. The four mark columns are read as a set, not individually.","groups":["Columns 2–5 (Free, Team, Business, Enterprise) form one visual family: same role (boolean presence), same content type (✓/—), same alignment, and they should share a similar width rhythm so the marks form clean vertical columns and the header row reads as a plan ladder.","Column 1 (Capability) stands alone as the row identifier and must be visually dominant over the mark family."],"keep_intact":["All four plan headers — 'Free', 'Team', 'Business', 'Enterprise' are single unbreakable words (36/44/72/83px), so their columns cannot be narrower than word+21px padding (57/65/93/104).","The longest unbreakable word in column 1 (91px) — column 1 must stay at least ~112px so no word overflows.","✓ and — marks must never be split or clipped; they need only a few px of text width, so their columns are governed by header width, not content."],"may_wrap":["Capability phrases in column 1 — they are multi-word noun phrases that wrap cleanly at spaces, and row height can absorb 2–4 lines without breaking row integrity.","Nothing else: the mark columns contain no wrappable text (headers are single words, cells are single glyphs)."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[190,57,65,93,104],"idea":"Text-first: hand every spare pixel to the capability column (only 3 lines per row, best for reading the phrases) and shrink each plan column to the exact width of its header word, accepting tight header gutters in exchange for the roomiest row headers."},{"name":"B","widths":[155,65,75,100,114],"idea":"Balanced ladder: a compromise where capability still wraps to only 3 lines while each plan column gets a little air beyond its header word, with widths stepping upward Free→Enterprise so the plan ladder reads as a deliberate progression rather than four random slots."},{"name":"C","widths":[112,90,96,104,107],"idea":"Mark-first: capability sits at its minimum safe width (4 lines, tall rows) so the four plan columns become near-equal, calm, evenly-spaced cells in which the ✓/— grid aligns into strong vertical stripes for quick cross-plan pattern spotting."}]}
